newsitem.title: ITALY: Neighbouring countries wary of Albanian exodus.
newsitem.headline: Neighbouring countries wary of Albanian exodus.

text.p: Albania's neighbours, fearful that the violent unrest gripping the tiny Balkan state may spark an uncontrollable exodus of refugees, are hoping -- without much optimism -- for a swift political solution.
Italian diplomatic sources complained on Wednesday that Albanian President Sali Berisha was unresponsive to outside appeals for a negotiated end to the uprising.
"We still hope to prevent a meltdown in Albania, but the authorities there are not helping us to help them," a diplomat at the Italian foreign ministry said.
Italy and Greece, which were swamped by tens of thousands of Albanians in 1991 after 45 years of Stalinist rule crumbled, have boosted patrols to try to head off a fresh wave of illegal immigration.
The Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia has ordered its army to increase combat readiness along the Albanian frontier.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini was quoted in a newspaper interview on Wednesday as saying that Italy would be prepared to send financial aid and troops to Albania to help maintain order.
"But to do all this we must have an Albanian government we can talk to," he told the daily La Repubblica.

Piero Fassino, a junior Italian foreign minister, told Reuters that soldiers would only be sent to Albania as part of a wider international initiative or else in limited operations to help evacuate stranded nationals.

The Albanian parliament declared a state of emergency at the weekend after an orgy of violence in the south, and has ordered the army to shoot armed rioters on sight. Eyewitnesses reported clashes between insurgents and army units on Wednesday.

Italy, Albania's largest trading partner, has been at the forefront of efforts to defuse the crisis and has put pressure on Berisha to create a cross-party administration to replace Aleksander Meksi's government, which resigned on Saturday.
Berisha rejected the call on Tuesday.

At Italy's request, officials from the European Union are due to discuss Albania at a meeting in Brussels on Thursday, but the Italians have been frustrated by the attitude of some of their EU partners.
"We cannot hide the fact that within the EU, Nordic states are keeping their distance from events in the Balkans," Dini told La Repubblica. "Agreements aren't the easiest thing."
Fassino warned that the rest of Europe would be making a serious error if it underestimated the problem.
"We believe that what is happening is very dangerous not just for Albania, but also for the whole Balkan region and therefore the rest of Europe," he said.
There are particular worries that the troubles could ignite smouldering discontent in large ethnic Albanian communities in the Serbian province of Kosovo and in Macedonia.

Greece is also concerned that the ethnic Greek minority in southern Albania might be victimised in any army crackdown. "You know there is a Greek minority in Albania and it is in our interest to support this minority if it is in danger," deputy Greek Foreign Minister Yiannos Kranidiotis said this week.

Greece has sent more security forces to guard its northern border, but an Italian diplomat said that if the situation in Albania deteriorated further, there would be little that anyone could do to prevent an influx of refugees.
"Obviously there is the risk of a mass exodus and we couldn't start shooting at people who were looking for protection," the official said.
